EDIT: I just noticed that there's vector negation happening for the `gyro_look` variable, I think that's the reason the values are inverted:
```gdscript
	# Perform gamepad gyro look.
	if not Input.is_action_pressed(&"freeze_gyro"):

		var gyro_look := -Vector2(gyro.y, gyro.x)
		_yaw -= gyro_look.x * GYRO_SENSITIVITY * 0.5 * delta
		_pitch += gyro_look.y * GYRO_SENSITIVITY * delta
```

Testing with the project Calinou linked ([physics_interpolation_gyro.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/23911248/physics_interpolation_gyro.zip)) on macOS Sequoia:

## DualSense (wired and wireless)
There is notable drift (mostly horizontal) when setting the controller down and not touching it. In the following video, I have the DualSense sitting on my desk, not touching it at all.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/555b0ef1-6c67-4428-b2d8-97dd909ace56

---

When I tilt the front of the controller (i.e., where the USB-C cable plugs in) *upwards*, the in-game camera tilts *downwards*, and vice versa.

In the following video, I first tilt the front of the controller upwards, then downwards; you can see that the in-game camera tilts downwards, then upwards.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/833bc8be-29f0-40c3-a4a4-aa7624ad172b

Similarly, if I rotate the controller right, my in-game camera rotates left. In this video, I rotate right first, then left:

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/98a5f404-e5f6-4b13-8d76-ca949d0bdc34

This could maybe be technically accurate, and the fix to make it "feel right" would be to invert how the camera in the demo project works instead?

---

Possibly combining both of these issues, if I have the controller sitting on my desk, tilt it up, and then set it back down (so no net rotation), the in-game camera *does* experience a net rotation:

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/1dfc2f26-c9c8-4b5d-a59c-63be8493282f


## Switch Pro Controller (wired and wireless)
Drift here seems more noticeable, and much more vertical:

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6e11dbb4-734d-4bff-a498-9252f28aeb3b

Tilting the front of the controller upwards/downwards has the same effect as the DualSense.

Unfortunately due to the vertical drift, I can't reliably test how 1:1 the net rotation is.

## Joy-Con (L) and (R) individually
They seem to work about the same as the Switch Pro Controller, including the drift being more vertical.

Note that when used separately, the Joy-Cons expect to be held horizontally.

## Joy-Con (L) and (R) together
When turning on the second Joy-Con after the first was already connected, Godot froze and I got this output in the terminal:
```
ERROR: Error opening gamepad at index 16: Couldn't find mapping for device (16)
   at: process_events (drivers/sdl/joypad_sdl.cpp:159)
ERROR: Error opening gamepad at index 17: Couldn't load stick calibration
   at: process_events (drivers/sdl/joypad_sdl.cpp:159)
ERROR: Error opening joystick at index 18: Joystick 18 not found
   at: process_events (drivers/sdl/joypad_sdl.cpp:168)
WARNING: 

Assertion failure at SDL_GetJoysticks (thirdparty/sdl/joystick/SDL_joystick.c:772), triggered 1 time:
  'joysticks[joystick_index] > 0'

Abort/Break/Retry/Ignore/AlwaysIgnore? [abriA] : 
```

I restarted Godot with both Joy-Cons connected, and then it seemed to work more or less the same as the Switch Pro Controller. The Joy-Con (R) is used for the gyroscope in this case, but it expects to be held vertically.

I did get some errors in the console this time around too, but they didn't seem to impact anything:
```
ERROR: Error opening gamepad at index 1: Couldn't find mapping for device (1)
   at: process_events (drivers/sdl/joypad_sdl.cpp:159)
ERROR: Error opening gamepad at index 2: Couldn't find mapping for device (2)
   at: process_events (drivers/sdl/joypad_sdl.cpp:159)
```
This sounds like a Joy-Con (and maybe SDL) specific issue, not a gyro issue, so it's probably best to discuss more in a separate thread 😅

Regarding the drift issues I experienced, I do also recall hearing someone on RocketChat say they'd done a thorough analysis of various controllers' gyroscopes, and found (at least) the Switch Pro Controller to be really bad at staying still. So what I encountered could well just be issues with those controllers and nothing in SDL or this PR.
Thank you for your reviews, Meorge, Calinou and AThousandShips! :)

Quoting an older comment, but I'm thinking about it again.
If in the future there are controllers with more sensors and if we are going to support them, maybe they also should be included in `has_joy_sensors()` and `set_joy_sensors_enabled()`?
Or maybe it's probably too early to think about though.

I would personally prefer to have them separated into their own sets of functions. If other sensors were added in the future, it's very possible people would not want to have both sets of sensors enabled with all of the overhead and power consumption that would entail.

As a more concrete example, consider a sensor that detects the heart rate of the player when their fingers are resting on the joypad's triggers. This would definitely qualify as a "sensor", and so I'd expect `has_joy_sensors()` to return `true` because of it, even if this joypad didn't have motion sensors. Even if it did have motion sensors, it's very likely that I would want to enable the heart-rate sensor without enabling the motion sensor, since the latter isn't applicable to my game. As such, I think having `set_joy_motion_sensors_enabled()` and `set_joy_hr_sensors_enabled()` would be more explicit, even if they are a bit verbose.

```gdscript
Input.set_joy_heart_rate_sensors_enabled(0, true)
Input.set_joy_motion_sensors_enabled(0, true)

print(Input.has_joy_heart_rate_sensors_sensors(0))
print(Input.has_joy_motion_sensors(0))
```

The methods could take in a bitfield, like so:
```gdscript
Input.set_joy_sensors_enabled(0, JOY_SENSOR_HEART_RATE, true)
Input.set_joy_sensors_enabled(0, JOY_SENSOR_MOTION, false)

print(Input.has_joy_sensors(0, JOY_SENSOR_HEART_RATE))
print(Input.has_joy_sensors(0, JOY_SENSOR_MOTION))
```
This keeps the number of unique methods in `Input` lower, and I think might generally be a bit easier to extend upon with new sensors as they become available, but it does make for longer lines than having dedicated methods to interface with individual sensors.

It occurred to me that `joy_motion` could be ambiguous, as [`InputEventJoypadMotion`](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_inputeventjoypadmotion.html) is an already-existing class that refers to joystick/analog trigger movement.
